vignette:
Karim, fifty-two years old, is an actor. For thirty years, the stage was his home—a place where he could inhabit any emotion, any life, and still remain himself. But that changed two years ago, when his wife, Layla, died in a car accident.

It happened during the final act of a sold-out performance. He was in the middle of a monologue—a grief-stricken father begging his son to come home—when he saw the stage manager’s face in the wings. Pale. Urgent. He finished the scene, because that’s what you do. The applause came. Then he walked offstage into a small, windowless dressing room, where a police officer told him the words he still hears every single night: *She didn’t survive.*

Now, he cannot watch car crashes in movies. He cannot drive past the intersection on Highland and Wilshire, even though it adds twenty minutes to his commute. He has not been able to perform a single scene involving a phone call, a ringing telephone, or a stage manager entering unexpectedly. Last month, his agent called with a role in a television drama—a father receiving news of his daughter’s illness. Karim hung up without saying goodbye. He spent the rest of the day on the floor of his living room, Layla’s favorite scarf pressed to his face, breathing in the vanishing scent of her perfume.

The nightmares started three weeks after she died. They are not dreams, really—they are rehearsals. He watches her car crumple from a dozen different angles, each time with a different soundtrack: the screech of tires, the crack of metal, the silence. Sometimes he wakes up shouting her name. Other times he wakes up already reaching for a phone that is not there. His sleep is broken; he averages maybe four hours, often less. He has not spent a full night in the bedroom they shared since the funeral. Now he sleeps on the couch, the television on low, because silence feels like a threat.

He still goes to auditions, but his body betrays him. His voice quavers on lines about love. His hands shake when a director asks him to stand too close. He used to be known for his raw, immediate emotional availability—a quality that made him a sought-after character actor. Now, when he is asked to cry on cue, the tears come, but they are not for the role. They are for Layla. He feels a familiar panic rise: the terror of being trapped in a feeling he cannot control. He often excuses himself, walks to the restroom, and stares at his reflection until the panic subsides.

He avoids his old friends from the theater company. They want to talk about Layla, about how brave he is, about how much they miss her. But talking about her makes her feel more dead. And when he does not talk about her, the guilt coils in his chest. He has stopped attending the annual memorial service at the theater. He tells himself he is busy. He is not busy.

Karim has not touched a script in three months. He has stopped answering his agent’s calls. The stack of unread plays on his nightstand has grown, but he cannot open them. Every page seems to have a character who loses someone. He spends most of his days sitting in the dark of his apartment, scrolling through old photos on his phone, reading the last text she sent him: *Break a leg, my love. I’ll be in the front row.* She was always in the front row. Now, when he imagines performing again, he sees an empty seat. A spotlight on an empty chair. And he cannot step onto the stage into that silence.
